strengths: Clearly motivated problem addressing real L2D limitations: poor OOD generalization, data inefficiency, and inability to leverage prior knowledge
Well-structured three-part technical approach with clean separation of concerns (behavior representation, expert-agnostic deferral, reduced annotations)
Strong and consistent empirical results across 6 diverse datasets with 4-28% improvements over L2D-Pop in high-diversity settings, particularly for OOD experts
Useful methodological contribution: AURSAC/AURDAC metrics address practical gap in evaluating L2D systems under variable deferral budgets
Theoretical soundness with convergence guarantees (Propositions 1-2) and formal characterization of expert-agnostic property (Proposition 3)
Practical features: ability to incorporate domain knowledge via priors, adapt to new experts without retraining, reduce query-level annotation requirements
weaknesses: CRITICAL: Unfair experimental comparison—EA-L2D is trained without query-level expert annotations while baselines use them, creating a fundamental information asymmetry that confounds results. Unclear if improvements stem from the method or data advantage

Limited technical novelty: Beta-Binomial conjugate modeling is standard Bayesian machinery; Propositions 1-2 follow straightforwardly from LLN and concentration inequalities; Proposition 3 is tautological (confirms design choices rather than proving properties)

No ablation studies on critical design choices: Why these 4 specific rejector inputs? Why weight loss by μ^E_{k=y}? Why selective activation via I[E*=y^Q]? How much improvement comes from reduced annotations vs. the Bayesian approach?

Prior incorporation limitations inadequately addressed: Figure 4 shows inaccurate priors significantly degrade performance (AURDAC drops from 0.503 to 0.427); eliciting calibrated expert self-assessments is known to be difficult in clinical practice, severely limiting real-world deployment

Artificial expert simulation oversimplifies realistic behavior: oracle on one class, probability p elsewhere, random otherwise. Real expert errors are more complex with systematic biases and correlated errors. No validation on real expert annotations

Incomplete mechanistic analysis: Why does expert-agnosticism specifically help OOD experts given it uses same four features? No error analysis, failure case discussion, or visualization of learned rejection functions across expert types

Limited experimental scope: multi-expertise experiments (§5.2) only on 2 datasets; no sensitivity analysis on context data size λ (varies 35-645); no investigation of context-size-performance relationships
Loss function design (Eq. 3) lacks justification: Selective activation I[E*=y^Q] is a significant relaxation from standard L2D objectives; weighting by μ^E_{k=y} has no theoretical motivation
Data efficiency claims overstated: Method still requires per-expert context data (~35-645 samples); only saves annotations on query data, not context data

Incomplete related work and baselines: Pop-Avg baseline appears somewhat strawman-ish; no comparison with other Bayesian or Dirichlet-based approaches; missing recent probabilistic expert modeling work

strengths: Addresses a relevant problem in Learning to Defer by handling experts with unseen expertise patterns
Comprehensive evaluation across 6 diverse datasets with systematic variation of expert diversity (p ∈ {0.2, 0.5, 0.8})
Introduces useful evaluation metrics (AURSAC, AURDAC) that provide more nuanced assessment of L2D systems across varying deferral budgets
Well-written paper with clear presentation and effective visualizations
Provides theoretical analysis via Propositions 1-3 with formal proofs
Demonstrates consistent improvements for OOD experts in high-diversity settings (particularly p=0.2 across datasets)
weaknesses: Core technical novelty is limited—applying standard Beta-Binomial conjugate priors to L2D is a straightforward Bayesian extension rather than a novel contribution
Loss function modification (Eq. 3) that only activates deferral when E* = y^Q lacks theoretical justification and represents an ad-hoc departure from principled Bayesian optimization

Unfair experimental comparison: EA-L2D still requires substantial context data with expert annotations (150-645 samples), and annotation savings vs. other methods are not clearly quantified; missing ablations with equal annotations

Weak theoretical guarantees: Propositions provide only asymptotic convergence (no finite-sample rates), Proposition 2 assumes knowing accuracy gaps in advance (unrealistic), and Proposition 3's proof of 'expert-agnostic' property is tautological
No statistical significance testing despite reporting standard deviations; several performance differences appear within margin of error (e.g., CIFAR-10 p=0.8: 0.90±0.01 vs 0.91±0.00)
Insufficient justification for key design choices: Why these 4 specific rejector inputs? Why neural network vs. simple rule? No ablation studies provided

Prior incorporation is underdeveloped: tested only on one dataset in simulation, paper acknowledges confidence calibration is 'rarely perfect in clinical practice,' and no real methodology for eliciting calibrated priors from experts
Large variance in OOD improvements across datasets suggests mechanism is dataset-dependent and not well-understood; some datasets show minimal gains (HAM10000, Breast Ultrasound at p=0.8)
Missing critical ablations: effect of context set size, sensitivity to prior strength s, necessity of loss modification, contribution of different rejector inputs
Unrealistic expert simulation: simulated experts with oracle performance on single expertise class don't reflect real expert behavior with correlated errors and distributed expertise

strengths: Addresses genuine limitation of prior work (L2D-Pop) with an elegant expert-agnostic solution using Bayesian modeling of expert behavior
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 6 diverse datasets with systematic variation of expert diversity and both ID/OOD expert scenarios
Strong and consistent empirical results with 1-16% improvements for seen experts and 4-28% for unseen experts, particularly robust OOD performance
Practical contributions including reduced reliance on complete expert annotations and novel incorporation of prior knowledge about expert performance
Theoretical justification via three propositions providing convergence guarantees and sample complexity bounds
Clear presentation with effective visualizations (Figures 1-2) and detailed algorithms facilitating reproducibility
weaknesses: Limited core technical novelty: applies standard conjugate Beta-Binomial Bayesian inference to L2D rather than introducing fundamentally new techniques
Exclusively synthetic expert evaluation limits real-world validity; actual expert behavior may exhibit more complex patterns than the assumed single-class expertise model
Oversimplified expert behavioral model assuming each expert has single expertise class E* with uniform accuracy on non-expertise classes; doesn't capture correlations or nuanced specialization
Loss function design (Eq. 3) not justified: uses hard indicator I[E*=y^Q] without ablation comparing to softer weighting schemes or justification
Rejector architecture underspecified and oversimplified: vague 'feedforward network' description and no ablations justifying why 4-input design is sufficient
Insufficient failure mode analysis: limited discussion of when method underperforms, no sensitivity analysis for context sample size λ, no treatment of ambiguous E* cases
Prior incorporation practical limitations: obtaining calibrated expert self-assessments is unreliable in practice (acknowledged in Section 6), limiting real-world applicability
Incomplete comparison with L2D-Pop: no analysis of whether poor OOD performance reflects fundamental limitations vs implementation details, missing ablations isolating EA-L2D contributions
Evaluation scope limited to image classification; generalization to other modalities where expert behavior patterns may differ is unexplored

strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing genuine limitation of prior L2D methods in adapting to unseen experts with novel specializations
Solid theoretical contributions including convergence guarantees (Prop. 1), sample complexity bounds (Prop. 2), and asymptotic characterization (Thm. C.3)
Comprehensive experimental evaluation with systematic ID/OOD expert splits, multiple datasets, ablation studies, and qualitative analysis (t-SNE visualization)
Practical benefits: eliminates query set annotations (reducing burden by E×N_Q), supports optional prior knowledge, computationally more efficient than meta-learning (O(n_C+K) vs O(N²_C d_r))
Produces interpretable expert representations through explicit class-wise statistical summaries rather than latent embeddings
Demonstrates robustness under combined expert and input distribution shift (HAM10000→BCN20000 evaluation)
weaknesses: Critical limitation: All experiments use simulated oracle-accuracy experts with highly artificial behavior (one peak class, probability p elsewhere); no validation on real expert panels undermines claims about real-world applicability in healthcare

Expert-agnostic property overstated: terminology misleading (means invariant to class labels, not agnostic to capabilities); Prop. 3's proof is tautological—of course statistical functions of statistics are invariant to label permutations
Limited technical novelty: Beta-Binomial models, LCB weighting, and uncertainty quantification are established techniques; main contribution is combination, not fundamentally new methods

Loss function design insufficiently justified: Eq. 4 uses binary indicator I[E*=y^Q] ignoring off-peak expertise; Theorem C.3 shows induced deferral rule differs from standard L2D but paper doesn't justify why alternative is superior
Gap between theory and practice: convergence guarantees require n_k→∞ but experiments use sparse context (n_E_C=60-165); no finite-sample analysis of rejector network training

Prior knowledge component underdeveloped: tested only in single scenario; Proposition 2 bounds not empirically validated; prior strength s=10 choice unjustified; missing sensitivity analysis to prior misspecification

Model assumptions unrealistic: assumes independent per-class expertise (real experts exhibit correlated competence); cannot model confidence calibration or class-pair dependencies common in medical domains
Incomplete baseline comparisons: Multi-Expert L2D cannot handle OOD by design; Pop-Avg is weak baseline; no comparison with uncertainty quantification or OOD detection literature
Computational efficiency claims lack empirical support: Section A.3 provides complexity analysis only, no actual runtime comparisons provided
Evaluation metrics coarse: AURSAC/AURDAC integrated over [0,1] lacks granularity; more analysis at specific operating regimes would strengthen claims

strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing real limitations of L2D-Pop (OOD generalization, annotation burden, lack of prior incorporation)
Solid theoretical contributions: convergence guarantees (Prop 1), sample complexity bounds for prior misspecification (Prop 2), asymptotic characterization (Thm C.3)
More interpretable explicit statistical expert representations compared to latent embeddings
Consistent OOD improvements: up to 28% relative gain on Blood Cells dataset with high expert diversity
Comprehensive experimental evaluation: 4 datasets, 5 research questions, ablation studies on LCB weighting and prior knowledge
Reduced annotation requirements (context-only labels vs. query set labels)
Insightful qualitative analysis of L2D-Pop latent space overfitting (Fig. 5)
weaknesses: Critical limitation: All experiments use oracle-based simulated experts with no real expert validation. Claims about practical deployment benefits lack human subject support.

Core novelty is incremental: Beta-Binomial modeling is straightforward conjugate model application; 'expert-agnosticism' oversells careful network input design rather than fundamental innovation. Proposition 3 merely formalizes that deterministic functions are deterministic.

Loss function modification (Eq. 4) introducing LCB weighting lacks proper ablation. No isolated comparison of: (1) standard vs. modified loss, (2) representation alone vs. with LCB, (3) contribution of each component.
Weak baseline comparisons: L2D-Pop is only SOTA for OOD setting; Pop-Avg introduced by authors; no comparison to simpler alternatives (empirical accuracies, fixed policies, standard L2D variants).

Design assumptions underexplored: Single expertise class assumption (E*=argmax_k μ_k) may limit experts with multiple unrelated specializations; Beta-Binomial assumes constant per-class accuracy without context-dependence.

Incomplete OOD generalization explanation: Proposition 3 proves structural invariance but doesn't formally establish OOD generalization; relies on intuition and qualitative Fig. 5 analysis rather than rigorous proof.

Prior knowledge experiments limited to one simulated scenario; results validate Proposition 2 but don't demonstrate novel practical benefits. Shows only expected behavior: good priors help, bad priors overcome with data.
Asymptotic rule (Theorem C.3) differs from standard Bayes-optimal L2D rule (defers on P(Y=k̄)θ̄_k̄ ≥ max_y P(Y=y)) but lacks justification for why this particular rule is preferable.

Hyperparameter selection not justified: α=1 for LCB weighting unchosen; context subset size n_C under-analyzed. Figure 7 shows anomalous non-monotonic OOD performance vs. context pool size, suggesting potential overfitting to simulated distributions (unexplained).
Limited scope: Only medical imaging datasets (all 4); only classification; only visual modality; generalization to other domains unclear. No real expert studies despite practical claims.

strengths: Novel expert-agnostic methodology: Using explicit Bayesian representations (Beta-Binomial models) instead of learned latent embeddings is creative and well-motivated, with formal justification via Proposition 3 and detailed theoretical analysis

Strong empirical results: Up to 28% relative improvement on OOD experts with consistent gains across 4 diverse medical datasets; L2D-Pop consistently shows ID→OOD degradation (marked with †) while EA-L2D avoids this

Comprehensive experimental evaluation: 5 research questions with rigorous statistical testing (paired t-tests), extensive supplementary experiments (distribution shift robustness RQ5, LCB weighting ablations), and honest ID/OOD performance reporting

Significant practical advantages: Eliminates need for E×N_Q query annotations (reducing burden by millions of labels), provides interpretability through explicit statistics, enables prior knowledge incorporation, and is computationally more efficient than L2D-Pop

Rigorous theoretical contributions: Proposition 1 (expertise identification with finite-sample bounds), Proposition 2 (sample complexity for prior misspecification), Theorem C.3 (asymptotic deferral rule characterization) with detailed proofs
Clear problem motivation: Identifies three concrete limitations of L2D-Pop and addresses them systematically with thoughtful solutions

Excellent presentation: Well-written with good intuitive explanations, informative figures (especially Fig. 5 showing L2D-Pop's latent space failure modes), and comprehensive appendix with implementation details
weaknesses: Limited real-world validation: All experiments use simulated experts following a specific oracle model (correct with probability p on specialty class, random otherwise), which may not capture heterogeneous instance-dependent expertise, correlated errors, or temporal drift. While acknowledged, this is the most critical gap for a high-stakes domain

Expert representation specificity: Beta-Binomial model assumes homogeneous per-class accuracy, but real expertise may be instance-dependent. Limited sensitivity analysis and ablations on whether alternative distributional assumptions would be more robust

Incomplete L2D-Pop analysis: Latent space visualization (Fig. 5) covers only one dataset/configuration; hypothesis about L2D-Pop overfitting lacks systematic investigation. Computational efficiency comparison is theoretical without actual wall-clock timing

Prior knowledge integration gaps: Limited practical guidance on obtaining reliable priors (expert self-assessment bias, aggregation strategies). Figure 4 shows recovery from completely misspecified priors but real scenarios involve partial misspecification
Rejector network underexplored: 6-layer MLP chosen without justification; no ablations on architecture depth/width, alternative input combinations, or sensitivity to design choices

Multi-expert system underspecified: RQ2 only varies number of classes per single expert; inference-time strategy for multiple experts unclear (which expert chosen when many available?); scalability to many experts unaddressed

Theory-practice gap: Finite-sample bounds in Proposition 1 depend critically on gap Δ between expert accuracies; when Δ is small (realistic), bounds become loose. Practical implications for typical medical scenarios not explored

Evaluation metric limitations: AURSAC/AURDAC are abstract; cost-sensitive evaluation with realistic medical costs (asymmetric costs for false deferral vs. missed deferral across different classes) not considered
Missing ablations: Unbalanced context data distribution, sparse context regime (N_C << 100), systematic sensitivity analysis over α ∈ [0, 2] in LCB weighting
Statistical rigor: Multiple comparisons across conditions (4 datasets × 3 p-values × 2 ID/OOD) without Bonferroni correction; some improvements statistically significant but modest in magnitude
